analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover mammograms, Pap tests, and colon and prostate cancer screening.
analysis.headline: The Cancer Screening Coverage Act, with 47 cosponsors including 9 Republicans, was sent to three House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or action in the Senate before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group health plans and individual health insurance to cover routine cancer screening: annual mammograms for women 40 and older, annual clinical breast exams, annual Pap tests and pelvic exams, colorectal screening starting at 50, and prostate screening starting at 50, with earlier or more frequent screening for people at high risk. It would also bar insurers from denying enrollment to avoid the requirement and from paying people or pressuring doctors to sidestep it. Plans could still charge deductibles and coinsurance, as long as the charges did not discriminate against these screenings. The bill died in House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and men with employer or individual health insurance who would otherwise pay out of pocket for mammograms, Pap tests, colon cancer screening, and prostate tests. Insured women 40 and older and adults 50 and older gain the most, since the bill sets specific screening schedules for them; people with family histories of cancer get screening at earlier ages.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers offering group coverage to pay for annual mammograms for women 40 and older (or younger women at high risk) and annual clinical breast exams, on terms no less favorable than other screening benefits [S3].

Requires coverage of annual Pap tests and pelvic exams for women 18 and older, colorectal screening (annual fecal occult blood tests, sigmoidoscopy every four years, and colonoscopy for high-risk patients) starting at age 50, and annual prostate screening starting at 50 [S3].
Extends the same screening requirements to insurance sold in the individual market, so people buying their own coverage are protected too [S3].
Bars plans from denying or ending someone's enrollment just to escape the mandate, from paying individuals to accept weaker coverage, and from penalizing doctors for providing covered screening [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group plans would pay for the added screening benefits, costs that flow into premiums shared by employers and workers. People at high risk of colon cancer, whose colonoscopies every two years are the most expensive item on the list, drive a meaningful share of the added cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows plans to keep charging deductibles and coinsurance on these screenings, so coverage would not necessarily mean free screening for patients [S3].
Mandated benefits add to premiums, a cost borne by employers and workers rather than the government, and the bill contains no offsetting funding [S3].

The screening schedule is fixed in statute, including annual prostate testing for men 50 and older, rather than left to doctors' judgment; routine PSA screening of older men has been debated for decades because it can lead to treatment of cancers that would never have caused harm.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: insurance coverage for proven screenings like mammography and colon cancer detection catches cancers earlier and saves lives, and the bill's anti-evasion rules close the obvious ways plans could dodge the mandate. The costs are a modest premium increase spread across all enrollees, and the bill's weaknesses are design choices rather than fatal flaws: patients could still face cost-sharing, and the rigid statutory schedule ignores evolving medical evidence. On balance the help to ordinary people outweighs the cost, which makes its quiet death more notable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and their subcommittees in April 1999, none of which ever held a hearing or a vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney of New York introduced the bill on March 25, 1999, joined by 47 cosponsors, including 9 Republicans and 1 Independent [S1].

It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and additionally to the Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means Committees, the standard first step for a health insurance mandate touching labor and tax law [S5].

Within a month it was sent to three subcommittees: Health and Environment (under Commerce) on April 12, Health (under Ways and Means) on April 19, and Employer-Employee Relations (under Education and the Workforce) on April 26 [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no subcommittee acted on it, and it never reached the House floor or the Senate; the final action in the record is the April 26, 1999 subcommittee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers who fund group plans came out ahead: they never had to add the mandated screening benefits or absorb the premium impact. Insured women and men kept paying out of pocket for screenings the bill would have covered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoided the mandate

for.name: Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks in the House and an extension of remarks supporting it.

for.name: 47 House cosponsors (37 of 211 Democrats, 9 of 223 Republicans, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support but no committee action followed.

against.name: House Commerce Committee (Chair Tom Bliley)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 25, 1999 and referred it to its Health and Environment Subcommittee on April 12; the committee never held a markup or vote on it.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means Committees (Chairs Bill Goodling and Bill Archer)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill alongside Commerce and referred it to their own subcommittees; neither committee acted on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Split the bill across three committees, a routing that let the session end without any of them acting on it; no committee chair in the majority brought it up.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: 37 of 211 Democrats, 9 of 223 Republicans, and 1 Independent signed on as cosponsors, but the Republican-controlled committees that held the bill never acted on it and no vote was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have required insurers to pay for a defined set of cancer screenings in both group and individual markets and barred them from steering around the requirement through enrollment denials, cash rebates, or pressure on doctors. Their financial interest was in not covering these services, which is the direct opposite of enrollees' interest in getting screened.

ERISA plans would have had to add the screening benefits to their packages, raising plan costs. Those costs would be shared with workers through premiums and reduced wages, but employers' interest in holding costs down ran against the mandate.

industries.industry: Screening providers (radiology, clinical labs, gastroenterology, oncology)
industries.note: A coverage mandate creates paying patients for mammography facilities, pathology labs, and endoscopy providers. When screening is covered, more people get it and get it earlier, which also serves patients.
